readings.title: Why Reddy Fox Has No Friends — the midnight feast
readings.challenge: Keep a list of who comes to the feast, what each brings, and what each secretly wants.
readings.focus: A friendly party on the outside hides envy and plans on the inside.
readings.context: From Mother West Wind’s Children (1911), Thornton W. Burgess’s second book of Green Meadows animal stories. The animals talk and plan like people. A feast is a big special meal; each guest is to bring the food he likes best, and many of these animals eat other animals. Envy is wanting what someone else has. A glutton is someone who eats far too much.
readings.contentNote: Several guests bring food they have stolen or killed, including a chicken from Farmer Brown and one of Mother Quack’s ducklings. The story tells it without detail.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Why Reddy Fox Has No Friends,” from the start to Jimmy Skunk’s plan for the chicken; opens “The Green Meadows lay peaceful and still. Mother Moon, sailing high overhead, looked down…”; closes “…Skunk began to think of a way to add the chicken of Reddy Fox to his own stolen eggs.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the Merry Little Breezes miss the midnight feast?
facilitatorNotes: It is night, and they are tucked in bed behind the Purple Hills.
evidence: Now they were safely tucked in bed behind the Purple Hills

questions.prompt: Which guests come with nothing to share? Give each one’s reason.
facilitatorNotes: Boomer the Nighthawk swallowed his insects as he caught them; Hooty the Owl is lazy and hides in the tree, uninvited; Shadow the Weasel would rather steal. Three different reasons, and only Boomer’s is innocent.
evidence: Hooty had not been invited and no one knew that he was there
he too went to the midnight spread with nothing but his appetite

questions.prompt: Which guests brought food they got honestly, and which brought stolen food?
facilitatorNotes: Little Joe Otter fished and Jerry Muskrat dug clams; Reddy’s chicken and Jimmy’s eggs were stolen. Children may argue about the cabbage, since the story does not say where Peter found it.
evidence: Jerry Muskrat brought up from the mud of the river bottom some fine fresh water clams
Jimmy Skunk stole three big eggs from the nest of old Gray Goose.

questions.prompt: Reddy Fox, Billy Mink and Jimmy Skunk each want someone else’s food. Who wants what?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy wants Billy’s duck, Billy wants Little Joe Otter’s trout, and Jimmy wants Reddy’s chicken: a circle of envy. Ask what might happen at a party like that.
evidence: his eyes danced and his heart swelled with envy

readings.title: Why Reddy Fox Has No Friends — sent away one by one
readings.challenge: Notice a repeated pattern, “No sooner had …”, and count the guests as they leave.
readings.focus: Reddy Fox uses each guest’s favourite food to send him away.
readings.context: Recap: the meadow folk have gathered at night under the Lone Pine for a feast, each bringing food. Reddy Fox wants Billy Mink’s duck, Billy wants Little Joe Otter’s trout, and Jimmy Skunk wants Reddy’s chicken. Hooty the Owl is hiding in the tree. A committee is someone given a job to do; an errand is a trip to fetch something.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Why Reddy Fox Has No Friends,” from the seating at the feast to Reddy Fox alone with the food; opens “Because Reddy Fox is the largest he was given the place of honor at the head of the table…”; closes “…been to get rid of all the others, and of how he would enjoy the feast all by himself.”.

questions.prompt: Reddy opens the feast with “brotherly love.” What is he really thinking about?
facilitatorNotes: Billy Mink’s duck: he looks at it hungrily the moment he stops speaking. His words and his eyes do not match.
evidence: we have met here to-night for a feast of brotherly love
Reddy Fox paused a moment to look hungrily at Billy Mink's duck.

questions.prompt: How does Reddy pick the right errand for each guest? Give two examples.
facilitatorNotes: He offers each one something he loves or is known for: a fast runner to fetch Bobby Coon, the egg-stealer to steal eggs, a fish for the otter, carrots for the rabbits, apples for Jerry Muskrat.
evidence: Now Peter Rabbit and Jumper the Hare are very fond of tender young carrots
Little Joe Otter listened and his mouth watered

questions.prompt: Billy Mink and Jimmy Skunk don’t want to go. Why do they go anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy asks in front of everyone, and refusing would look rude or selfish. Some children may say they were afraid of Reddy.
evidence: there was nothing for him to do but to yield as gracefully as he could

questions.prompt: Reddy thinks he is alone at last. Who has he forgotten?
facilitatorNotes: Shadow the Weasel, who has already eaten the goose eggs and slipped away, and Hooty the Owl, still hidden in the Lone Pine. Ask what Hooty might do next.
evidence: At least he thought himself alone

readings.title: Why Reddy Fox Has No Friends — the shadow in the pine
readings.challenge: Follow a mystery from Reddy Fox’s side when you already know the answer.
readings.focus: The trickster is tricked, and only the honest guests end the night content.
readings.context: Recap: Reddy Fox sent every guest away from the midnight feast on a false errand so that he could eat everything himself. Shadow the Weasel slipped off after secretly eating the goose eggs. Reddy thinks he is alone, but Hooty the Owl has been hiding in the Lone Pine all along. A conscience is the feeling inside that tells you whether you have done right.
readings.contentNote: Hooty the Owl carries off the food in the dark. Reddy Fox is badly frightened, and the hungry animals quarrel.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Why Reddy Fox Has No Friends,” from the shadow dropping out of the Lone Pine to the end of the chapter; opens “As Reddy Fox stooped to pick up Billy Mink's duck, a great shadow dropped softly, oh so…”; closes “And this is why Reddy Fox has no true friends on the Green Meadows.”.

questions.prompt: What is the “great shadow” that drops out of the Lone Pine? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: Hooty the Owl: he flies without a sound, he was hiding in that tree, and the last lines say his stomach is full of chicken, duck and trout.
evidence: without the teeniest, weeniest bit of noise
his stomach was very full of chicken and duck and trout

questions.prompt: Why is Reddy Fox so jumpy that he leaps a foot off the ground at Bowser’s bark?
facilitatorNotes: His food is vanishing without a sound or a smell, and the story says dishonest people are quick to suspect others. A thief is afraid of thieves.
evidence: Reddy Fox is very suspicious, as people who are not honest themselves are very apt to be

questions.prompt: The others decide Reddy Fox is the thief. Are they right?
facilitatorNotes: He did not eat the food; Hooty did. But he did send them away on false errands to have it all himself. They are wrong about what happened and right about his plan.
evidence: Reddy Fox is the thief!
had sent them all away on false errands that he might have the feast all to himself

questions.prompt: Why does Mother Moon smile at Peter, Jumper and Jerry Muskrat?
facilitatorNotes: They did no harm to anyone and have a clear conscience, and they still have the food they brought.
evidence: for she knew that each had a clear conscience, for they had done no harm to anyone

readings.title: Reddy Fox Disobeys — barking at the moon
readings.challenge: Notice a promise made every night and broken every night.
readings.focus: Reddy cannot explain why he barks, but he learns what his mother’s warning was for.
readings.context: From Mother West Wind’s Children (1911), Thornton W. Burgess’s second book of Green Meadows animal stories. The animals talk and plan like people. This story happens in winter, when the meadows are white with snow. Bowser the Hound is Farmer Brown’s hunting dog, kept on a chain at night. To slip a collar is to wriggle out of it. In full cry means barking loudly while chasing.
readings.contentNote: Bowser the Hound chases Reddy Fox to catch him, and Reddy fears that Farmer Brown would kill his whole family if Bowser found their home.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Reddy Fox Disobeys,” from the start to Bowser closing in on Reddy; opens “On the brow of the hill by the Lone Pine sat Reddy Fox. Every few moments he pointed his…”; closes “…doubled this way and that way, and all the time Bowser the Hound got closer and closer.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mother Fox warn Reddy about every night, and what does Reddy promise?
facilitatorNotes: That noisy children come to no good end; he promises to stop barking, and every night forgets.
evidence: noisy children would come to no good end
every night Reddy had promised that he would bark no more

questions.prompt: Why does Bowser think Reddy is making fun of him?
facilitatorNotes: Every night they bark back and forth across the meadows. Some children will say Reddy was not mocking at all, since “he just had to” bark; both readings fit.
evidence: Bowser the Hound knew, too, and he made up his mind that Reddy Fox was making fun of him.

questions.prompt: When the chase starts, why can’t Reddy just run home?
facilitatorNotes: Bowser would follow him and lead Farmer Brown to the den, putting his whole family in danger. Even while scared, Reddy thinks of them.
evidence: for that would tell Bowser where he lived

questions.prompt: How does the writer show that Reddy is getting tired?
facilitatorNotes: His breath grows short and comes in pants, and his proud bushy tail grows heavy.
evidence: the longer he ran, the shorter his breath grew
His bushy tail, of which he was so proud, had become very heavy.

readings.title: Reddy Fox Disobeys — Mother Fox’s trick
readings.challenge: Follow a plan step by step and say why each step works.
readings.focus: Mother Fox uses what she knows about Bowser’s nose and slow thinking to save her son.
readings.context: Recap: Reddy Fox kept barking at the moon though Mother Fox warned him not to. Tonight Bowser the Hound slipped his collar and chased him across the snowy meadows, and Reddy, nearly worn out, could not run home without showing Bowser where his family lived. A shock of corn is a bundle of cornstalks standing in a field. Scent is the smell an animal leaves behind it. The crotch of a tree is where a branch meets the trunk.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Reddy Fox Disobeys,” from Mother Fox hearing the chase to the end of the chapter; opens “Now way off on the hill behind the White Meadows Mother Fox had been hunting for her…”; closes “…tired and very sorrowful, and since that time Reddy Fox has never barked at the moon.”.

questions.prompt: How does Mother Fox tell Reddy she is coming to help?
facilitatorNotes: She barks twice. Reddy knows her bark and finds the strength to run faster.
evidence: she barked twice to tell Reddy that she would help him

questions.prompt: Why does Bowser chase Mother Fox instead of Reddy?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps his nose on the track, looks up, sees a fox sitting there and thinks it is Reddy. The story says twice that he thinks slowly.
evidence: But Bowser the Hound thinks slowly.

questions.prompt: Why does Mother Fox run along the stone wall and then jump into the apple tree?
facilitatorNotes: Stones hold little scent, the long jumps break her trail, and the tree hides her where she can watch.
evidence: She knew that stones do not carry the scent well

questions.prompt: Reddy never barks at the moon again. What do you think changed his mind?
facilitatorNotes: The fright of the chase, his mother’s rescue, or the punishment waiting at home. Accept any answer tied to how he felt: ashamed, tired and sorrowful.
evidence: very much ashamed, very tired and very sorrowful
since that time Reddy Fox has never barked at the moon
